facts.statement: The genus Protoceratops was described by Granger and Gregory in 1923.
facts.quote: authority: Granger & Gregory, 1923

facts.statement: Protoceratops lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 75 to 71 million years ago.
facts.quote: lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous, around 75 to 71 million years ago

facts.statement: Protoceratops were small ceratopsians reaching lengths of 2 to 2.5 meters and weighing between 62 and 104 kilograms.
facts.quote: Protoceratops were small ceratopsians, up to 2 - 2.5 m long and around 62 - 104 kg in body mass

facts.statement: Adult Protoceratops were primarily quadrupedal, though juveniles could walk bipedally if needed.
facts.quote: While adults were largely quadrupedal, juveniles had the capacity to walk around bipedally if necessary

facts.statement: Protoceratops are characterized by a proportionally large skull, a short stiff neck, and a neck frill.
facts.quote: They were characterized by a proportionally large skull, short and stiff neck, and neck frill

facts.statement: The neck frill of Protoceratops was likely used for display, intraspecific combat, neck protection, and anchoring jaw muscles.
facts.quote: The frill was likely used for display or intraspecific combat, as well as protection of the neck and anchoring of jaw muscles

facts.statement: Protoceratops possessed a horn-like structure over the nose that was single in P. andrewsi but double and paired in P. hellenikorhinus.
facts.quote: A horn-like structure was present over the nose, which varied from a single structure in P. andrewsi to a double, paired structure in P. hellenikorhinus

facts.statement: Protoceratops were herbivores with prominent jaws and teeth adapted for chopping foliage and plant material.
facts.quote: Protoceratops, like many other ceratopsians, were herbivores equipped with prominent jaws and teeth suited for chopping foliage and other plant material

facts.statement: Protoceratops appear to have cared for their young and laid soft-shelled eggs, a rare trait among dinosaurs.
facts.quote: They appear to have cared for their young. They laid soft-shelled eggs, a rare occurrence in dinosaurs

facts.statement: Protoceratops were hunted by Velociraptor, evidenced by the famous 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen showing them locked in combat.
facts.quote: Protoceratops were hunted by Velociraptor, and one particularly famous specimen (the Fighting Dinosaurs) preserves a pair of them locked in combat

facts.statement: Protoceratops were once thought to be nocturnal due to their large scleral rings, but are now believed to be cathemeral (active at dawn and dusk).
facts.quote: Protoceratops used to be characterized as nocturnal because of the large scleral ring around the eye, but they are now thought to have been cathemeral (active at dawn and dusk)

facts.statement: On September 2, photographer James B. Shackelford discovered the holotype skull (AMNH 6251) of Protoceratops in reddish sandstones.
facts.quote: On 2 September, the photographer James B. Shackelford discovered a partial juvenile skull—which would become the holotype specimen (AMNH 6251) of Protoceratops—in reddish sandstones

facts.statement: Granger and Gregory agreed with Osborn that further exploration of Asia could resolve major evolutionary gaps in the fossil record.
facts.quote: The co-authors also agreed with Osborn that Asia, if more thoroughly explored, could solve many major evolutionary gaps in the fossil record

facts.statement: Because Protoceratops was considered more primitive than other known ceratopsians, Granger and Gregory established the family Protoceratopsidae, characterized by the lack of horns.
facts.quote: Since Protoceratops was more primitive than any other known ceratopsian at that time, Granger and Gregory coined the new family Protoceratopsidae, mostly characterized by the lack of horns

facts.statement: In 1963, Mongolian paleontologist Demberelyin Dashzeveg reported the discovery of the Tugriken Shireh locality in the Djadokhta Formation.
facts.quote: In 1963, the Mongolian paleontologist Demberelyin Dashzeveg reported the discovery of a new fossiliferous locality of the Djadokhta Formation: Tugriken Shireh

facts.statement: It was initially believed that Protoceratops was an ancestor of ankylosaurians and larger ceratopsians like Triceratops, but this view changed after the discovery of other protoceratopsids.
facts.quote: Protoceratops was initially believed to be an ancestor of ankylosaurians and larger ceratopsians, such as Triceratops and relatives, until the discoveries of other protoceratopsids

facts.statement: Protoceratops remains were found in the 1970s in the Khulsan locality of the Barun Goyot Formation in Mongolia by Polish-Mongolian expeditions.
facts.quote: Protoceratopsid remains were recovered in the 1970s from the Khulsan locality of the Barun Goyot Formation, Mongolia, during the work of several Polish-Mongolian paleontological expeditions.

facts.statement: In 1975, Polish paleontologists Teresa Maryańska and Halszka Osmólska described the species Protoceratops kozlowskii.
facts.quote: In 1975, Polish paleontologists Teresa Maryańska and Halszka Osmólska described a second species of Protoceratops which they named P. kozlowskii.

facts.statement: In 2001, Oliver Lambert and colleagues named the new species Protoceratops hellenikorhinus.
facts.quote: In 2001 Oliver Lambert with colleagues named a new and distinct species of Protoceratops, P. hellenikorhinus.

facts.statement: The first remains of Protoceratops hellenikorhinus were collected in 1995 and 1996 from the Bayan Mandahu Formation in Inner Mongolia by Sino-Belgian expeditions.
facts.quote: The first known remains of P. hellenikorhinus were collected from the Bayan Mandahu locality of the Bayan Mandahu Formation, Inner Mongolia, in 1995 and 1996 during Sino-Belgian paleontological expeditions.

facts.statement: In 2006, Peter Makovicky and Mark A. Norell suggested that Bainoceratops might be a synonym of Protoceratops.
facts.quote: In 2006 North American paleontologists Peter Makovicky and Mark A. Norell suggested that Bainoceratops may be synonymous with Protoceratops

facts.statement: In 1923, Henry Fairfield Andrews and his team discovered the holotype of Oviraptor near a nest of dinosaur eggs in the Djadokhta Formation.
facts.quote: As part of the Third Central Asiatic Expedition of 1923, Andrews and team discovered the holotype specimen of Oviraptor in association with some of the first known fossilized dinosaur eggs (nest AMNH 6508), in the Djadokhta Formation.

facts.statement: Early researchers believed the eggs found near Oviraptor belonged to Protoceratops because of the dinosaur's high abundance in the area.
facts.quote: due to the proximity and high abundance of Protoceratops in the formation, these eggs were believed at the time to belong to this dinosaur.

facts.statement: In 1994, Norell and colleagues found an oviraptorid embryo in an egg, proving that the eggs previously thought to belong to Protoceratops actually belonged to Oviraptor.
facts.quote: However, also during 1994, Norell and colleagues reported and briefly described a fossilized theropod embryo inside an egg (MPC-D 100/971) from the Djadokhta Formation. They identified this embryo as an oviraptorid dinosaur and the eggshell, upon close examination, turned out be that of elongatoolithid eggs and thereby the oofamily Elongatoolithidae was concluded to represent the eggs of oviraptorids.

facts.statement: In 2008, Darla K. Zelenitsky and François Therrien concluded that the egg genus Protoceratopsidovum belonged to a maniraptoran dinosaur more derived than oviraptorids, not Protoceratops.
facts.quote: Moreover, phylogenetic analyses published in 2008 by Darla K. Zelenitsky and François Therrien have shown that Protoceratopsidovum represents the eggs of a maniraptoran more derived than oviraptorids and not Protoceratops.

facts.statement: In 2011, David E. Fastovsky and colleagues described an authentic nest of Protoceratops.
facts.quote: Nevertheless, in 2011 an authentic nest of Protoceratops was reported and described by David E. Fastovsky and colleagues.

facts.statement: In 2017, Gregory M. Erickson and team reported an egg clutch with embryos from Protoceratops at the Ukhaa Tolgod locality.
facts.quote: Gregory M. Erickson and team in 2017 reported an embryo-bearing egg clutch (MPC-D 100/1021) of Protoceratops from the also fossiliferous Ukhaa Tolgod locality, discovered during paleontological expeditions of the American Museum of Natural History and Mongolian Academy of Sciences.

facts.statement: In 2020, Norell and colleagues found evidence that the eggs of a Protoceratops clutch had a soft-shelled composition.
facts.quote: Norell with colleagues in 2020 examined fossilized remains around the eggs of this clutch which indicate a soft-shelled composition.

facts.statement: The 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen preserves a Protoceratops and a Velociraptor fossilized together, providing direct evidence of predator-prey behavior.
facts.quote: The Fighting Dinosaurs specimen preserves a Protoceratops (MPC-D 100/512) and Velociraptor (MPC-D 100/25) fossilized in combat and provides an important window regarding direct evidence of predator-prey behavior in non-avian dinosaurs.

facts.statement: On August 3, fossils of Protoceratops and Velociraptor were found at the Tugriken Shire locality in the Djadokhta Formation.
facts.quote: During fieldwork on 3 August several fossils of Protoceratops and Velociraptor were found at the Tugriken Shire locality (Djadokhta Formation) including a block containing one of each.

facts.statement: A drowning hypothesis for the burial of the 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen is considered unlikely due to the arid environment of the Djadokhta Formation.
facts.quote: Though a drowning scenario has been proposed by Barsbold, such a hypothesis is considered unlikely given the arid paleoenvironments of the Djadokhta Formation.

facts.statement: A nearly complete Protoceratops skeleton was collected at the Flaming Cliffs during the Third Central Asiatic Expedition in 1923.
facts.quote: During the Third Central Asiatic Expedition in 1923, a nearly complete Protoceratops skeleton (specimen AMNH 6418) was collected at the Flaming Cliffs.

facts.statement: In 2022, Phil R. Bell and colleagues described potential soft tissues of Protoceratops based on historical photographs.
facts.quote: In 2022 Phil R. Bell and colleagues briefly described these potential soft tissues based on the photographs provided by Brown and Schlaikjer, as well as other ceratopsian soft tissues.

facts.statement: An articulated subadult Protoceratops skeleton was collected from the Bayn Dzak locality in 1965.
facts.quote: In 1965 an articulated subadult Protoceratops skeleton (specimen ZPAL Mg D-II/3) was collected from the Bayn Dzak locality of the Djadokhta Formation.

facts.statement: A fossilized footprint associated with a Protoceratops skeleton was first reported in 2012 by Grzegorz Niedźwiedzki and colleagues.
facts.quote: This footprint was described in 2012 by Grzegorz Niedźwiedzki and colleagues who considered it to represent one of the first reported finds of a dinosaur footprint in association with an articulated skeleton, and also the first one reported for Protoceratops.

facts.statement: Protoceratops species were small ceratopsians, reaching lengths of 2 to 2.5 meters and masses of 62 to 104 kilograms.
facts.quote: Protoceratops was a relatively small-sized ceratopsian, with both P. andrewsi and P. hellenikorhinus estimated up to 2 - 2.5 m in length, and around 62 - 104 kg in body mass.

facts.statement: P. andrewsi is characterized by two premaxillary teeth, a low and long snout, a single pointed nasal horn, and a slightly curved dentary edge.
facts.quote: P. andrewsi – Two teeth were present at the premaxilla; the snout was low and long; the nasal horn was a single, pointed structure; the bottom edge of the dentary was slightly curved.

facts.statement: P. hellenikorhinus lacks premaxillary teeth, has a tall and broad snout, a nasal horn divided into two ridges, and a straight dentary edge.
facts.quote: P. hellenikorhinus – Absence of premaxillary teeth; the snout was tall and broad; the nasal horn was divided into two pointed ridges; the bottom edge of the dentary was straight.

facts.statement: The skull of P. hellenikorhinus had a total length of about 70 centimeters.
facts.quote: On the other hand P. hellenikorhinus had a total skull length of about 70 cm.

facts.statement: The rear of the Protoceratops skull formed a pronounced neck frill composed mainly of parietal and squamosal bones.
facts.quote: The rear of the skull gave form to a pronounced neck frill (also known as "parietal frill") mostly composed of the parietal and squamosal bones.

facts.statement: The parietal bones formed the posterior part of the skull and the main elements of the frill, appearing triangular from above and joined by the frontals.
facts.quote: The parietals were the posteriormost bones of the skull and major elements of the frill. In a top view they had a triangular shape and were joined by the frontals (bones of the skull roof).

facts.statement: The deep and sharply developed jugal, along with the quadratojugal, formed a horn-like extension pointing downward at the sides of the skull.
facts.quote: The jugal was deep and sharply developed and along with the quadratojugal they formed a horn-like extension that pointed to below at the lateral sides of the skull.

facts.statement: Coarse surfaces around the epijugal indicate it was covered by a horny sheath.
facts.quote: The surfaces around the epijugal were coarse, indicating that it was covered by a horny sheath.

facts.statement: In P. hellenikorhinus, the palpebral bone protruded upwards to create a small horn-like structure above the eye socket.
facts.quote: The palpebral (small spur-like bone) joined the prefrontal over the front of the orbit (eye socket). In P. hellenikorhinus the palpebral protruded upwards from the prefrontal, just above the orbit and slightly meeting the frontal, creating a small horn-like structure.

facts.statement: Protoceratops had well-developed binocular vision due to its forward-facing, closely located orbits and narrow snout.
facts.quote: The forward facing and closely located orbits combined with a narrow snout, gave Protoceratops a well-developed binocular vision.

facts.statement: The toothless, high, and triangular rostral bone had a rough texture indicating the presence of a horny beak.
facts.quote: The rostral bone was devoid of teeth, high and triangular in shape. It had a sharp end and rough texture, which reflects that a rhamphotheca (horny beak) was present.

facts.statement: Protoceratops had large orbits measuring around 5 centimeters in diameter with irregular shapes varying by individual.
facts.quote: Protoceratops had large orbits, which measured around 5 cm in diameter and had irregular shapes depending on the individual.

facts.statement: Protoceratops possessed leaf-shaped dentary and maxillary teeth with serrated edges.
facts.quote: Protoceratops had leaf-shaped dentary and maxillary teeth that bore several denticles (serrations) on their respective edges.

facts.statement: The dentary and maxillary teeth of Protoceratops showed marked homodonty, sharing similar shapes and sizes.
facts.quote: Both dentary and maxillary teeth presented marked homodonty—a dental condition where the teeth share a similar shape and size.

facts.statement: P. andrewsi had two small, peg-to-spike-like teeth located on the underside of each premaxilla.
facts.quote: P. andrewsi bore two small, peg to spike-like teeth that were located on the underside of each premaxilla.

facts.statement: Unlike later ceratopsians, Protoceratops lacked well-developed horns.

facts.statement: Protoceratops reached a length of 1.8 meters, a height of 60 centimeters at the hips, and weighed 60 kilograms.
facts.quote: El Protoceratops llegó a medir 1,8 metros de largo, con 60 centímetros de alto hasta la cruz, y a pesar 60 kilogramos

facts.statement: The first Protoceratops remains were found in 1922 by an expedition led by American explorer Roy Chapman Andrews in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia.

facts.statement: Walter Granger and W. K. Gregory formally described the type species P. andrewsi in 1923.

facts.statement: In 1971, a fossil of Protoceratops entangled in combat with a Velociraptor was found in the Djadochta Formation in Omnogov, Mongolia.

facts.statement: Polish paleontologists Teresa Maryanska and Halszka Osmólska described a second species, P. kozlowskii, from the Campanian of Mongolia in 1975.

facts.statement: A second valid species, P. hellenikorhinus, was named in 2001 from the Bayan Mandahu Formation in Inner Mongolia, China.

facts.statement: In 2011, it was discovered that a Protoceratops specimen originally unearthed in 1965 preserved footprints of the animal.

facts.statement: Researchers have recognized two species of Protoceratops, P. andrewsi and P. hellenikorhinus, based partly on their respective sizes.

facts.statement: Some revisions, such as those by Peter Dodson, attribute differences in the size and shape of cranial bones like the parietal and squamosal to sexual dimorphism and age.

facts.statement: The exact size and shape of the neck frill varied among individuals, with some having short, compact frills and others having frills nearly half the length of the skull.

facts.statement: P. kozlowskii consisted of incomplete juvenile remains and is now considered a junior synonym of Bagaceratops rozhdestvenskyi.

facts.statement: Protoceratops resembled ceratopsids but had limb proportions suited for running, smaller frills, and lacked large horns.

facts.statement: In 1998, Paul Sereno defined Protoceratopsidae as the node-based clade including all ceratopsians more closely related to Protoceratops than to Triceratops.

facts.statement: Bainoceratops may be considered a more modern synonym of Protoceratops.
